frase_gancho.texto: Two square pieces of cloth that, joined together, form a cape and a world of embroidery.

puente_narrativo.texto: From the Otomí quechquémitl we move on to the formal dress of their neighbors, the Mazahua women. Look for a long red wool skirt, pleated at the waist, with a wide embroidered sash and large silver earrings.

guion_corto.texto: This quechquémitl comes from an Otomí community in central Mexico and is woven on a backstrap loom. It is a garment that covers the shoulders, made from two rectangular panels joined so that they form a diamond, with one point in front and another in back. Look at the embroidery: stars, birds, and flowers, worked in colored wool on white cotton, with a technique called pepenado. The quechquémitl is a very old garment, from before the arrival of the Spanish. Today it remains a symbol of Otomí women, who wear it at festivals and in everyday life. Every stitch shows the care and patience of the person who made it.

guion_largo.texto:
If the shawl is the great mestizo garment, the quechquémitl is the great Indigenous garment. Its name comes from Nahuatl: “quechtli” means neck and “quemitl” means garment. It is, quite literally, a garment for the neck. And its shape is ingenious: two rectangular panels joined so that, when placed over the shoulders, two points fall, one in front and one down the back. Nothing is cut from the cloth.

It is an ancient garment. It appears in sculptures from the Gulf Coast, such as those of the Huastec women, and in the images of goddesses in the codices of ancient Mexico. When an Otomí woman puts one on, she wears a form that was already known when the pyramids were being raised. It is another example of something that survived because it kept being used, and not because it sat in a display case.

The Otomí have lived in the center of the country for a very long time. It is thought that they occupied these lands long before the Mexica, and that their language was one of those heard when Teotihuacán was great. Today their largest concentration is in the Mezquital Valley, in Hidalgo, and in the highlands of Puebla, Veracruz, and Querétaro.

Look closely at the embroidery. The technique is called pepenado: the embroiderer counts the threads of the cotton cloth and covers them with wool, so that the design is born from the weave itself. The motifs are stars, birds, and flowers, and sometimes a tree that is interpreted as the tree of life. Every quechquémitl is different, because every embroiderer invents a little.

In the state of Hidalgo, in the town of Tenango de Doria, the Otomí embroideries of animals and plants have become famous under the name “tenangos.” They are another form of the same tradition: lively figures in intense colors that tell the story of a landscape. And in San Pablito, in the highlands of Puebla, there is another famous Otomí community, the home of [Amate Paper](mna_s16_papel_amate_sanpablito), which you will see in the Puebla Highlands Hall.

There are quechquémitls of wool, of cotton, and of very fine gauze, with embroidery or with brocade, and each region has its own style and its own way of wearing it. All of them share the idea of the two points. In the highlands of Puebla you will see a garment of fine gauze, the [huipil of Cuetzalan](mna_s16_huipil_cuetzalan), from the same family of textile ideas.

Think about the time it takes. First the panels must be woven on the backstrap loom, the technique you saw in the [textile collection](mna_s12_acervo_textil). Then comes the embroidery, stitch by stitch, until the whole surface is covered. Some quechquémitls take months. When the work is finished, the garment is no longer just clothing: it is a piece that identifies the person who wears it as part of her people and her family.

In a hall full of clothing, this one has something special: it tells a story of continuity. The goddesses of the codices wore the quechquémitl; the women of today do too. Between them lie hundreds of years and not a single pause.

texto: Find the two points of the quechquémitl: one in front and one down the back
Look closely at the embroidery of stars, birds, and flowers
Notice how the colored wool stands out against the white cotton

texto.Technique/Material: Cotton woven on a backstrap loom and embroidered in picked-thread technique with wool
texto.Function: Ceremonial and everyday dress of high prestige for women

texto.pregunta: Myth: The quechquémitl is a garment invented after the arrival of the Spanish.
texto.respuesta: Reality: It is a very old garment, from before the conquest: it appears in sculptures and in the codices, and it is still worn today.
